title: Diwali: the row of lamps
hook: Rama comes home after fourteen years, and a whole city lights lamps to show him the way

segments.voice: Yesterday: Navaratri, nine nights of the Goddess, and a tenth day when the good wins. Nine nights, then the dawn.

You already know the night this festival remembers: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana flying home after fourteen years, Bharata waiting with the sandals, and the people of Ayodhya lighting lamps on every wall so he could find his way. Now it's here, for real. The darkest night of the autumn month. The house has been cleaned for days. Someone's drawing a pattern in colored powder on the doorstep. There are sweets in boxes on every surface. And as the sun goes down, a whole country, and families all over the world, start lighting little clay lamps, one after another after another.
screen: `THE NIGHT YOU ALREADY KNOW.` → `COLORED POWDER ON THE DOORSTEP.` → `ONE LAMP, THEN ANOTHER.`

segments.voice: In many places, Diwali is five days, not one. It often starts with a day for buying something new, often a little metal, for good fortune. Then a day that remembers a victory over a demon of darkness. Then the main night, on the new moon, when many families worship Lakshmi, the goddess of fortune and well-being, and leave their lights and doors open so she'll come in. Then a day for Krishna lifting a mountain to shelter his village, sometimes marked with a mountain of food. And the fifth day is for brothers and sisters. Not everyone lights the lamps for the same story. In much of the north, it's Rama coming home. In much of the south, it's Krishna defeating a demon king called Narakasura, and people wake before dawn to bathe and celebrate. For many business families, it's Lakshmi, and the start of a new account year. Neighbors share the season too: Jains remember the day Mahavira attained liberation, and Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas, the return of Guru Hargobind from prison. Different stories, the same lamps. Why lamps on the darkest night? An old line from the Upanishads, still chanted today, asks to be led from the unreal to the real, from darkness to light, from death to what doesn't die. Diwali puts that on a windowsill. You don't argue with the dark. You light a small flame in it, and then another, until someone coming home can see the way.
screen: `FIVE DAYS, NOT ONE.` · `LAKSHMI ON THE DARKEST NIGHT.` · `DIFFERENT STORIES, THE SAME LAMPS.` · `FROM DARKNESS, LEAD ME TO LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Light one light if you can: a candle, a small lamp, even a phone screen turned toward you. Think of someone far from home right now, a child away or a friend in another country, or someone lost or lonely who has drifted from the people who love them. Picture your light in a window they could see; you're not pulling them home, just showing the way.
Diwali. The row of lamps, five days, many stories, lit on the darkest night of the month.
Your line: light the way home. One small flame, then another. Day eighty-one, done.

howItsDone: For Diwali, Hindu families clean and decorate their homes, draw rangoli patterns at the door, light rows of clay lamps, worship Lakshmi on the new-moon night, share sweets, and visit relatives; customs and the stories told vary by region over the festival's five days.
